title: Diverse efficiency of observable optimization for four-level quantum systems with higher-order traps
abstract: In this work, we perform an analytical and numerical analysis of quantum landscapes for controlling special four-level quantum systems for which we prove that the null control is a five-order trap: a $V-V$ system and an anharmonic system. As a control goal, an observable optimization is considered. The rigorous theoretical analysis is followed by the numerical experiments based on the GRadient Ascent Pulse Engineering (GRAPE) algorithm and Gradient Projection Method (GPM), performed to investigate the behavior of the efficiency of optimization for unconstrained (using GRAPE) and constrained (using GPM) controls. As the main result, we observe an interesting phenomenon with a diverse behavior of the optimization efficiency depending on the system Hamiltonian -- sharp increase of the optimization efficiency up to 100% at certain distance from the null control for a V-V system, while much slower and less significant increase (and even small decrease) for a system with the chain interaction. This sharp difference might be related with the fine structure of the subspace of controls where second derivative of the objective functional is zero.
summary: This paper investigates optimizing observables in four-level quantum systems using advanced quantum control techniques. It proves that the null control acts as a high-order trap and numerically demonstrates that the efficiency of finding optimal controls varies dramatically depending on whether the system Hamiltonian resembles a V-V structure or a chain interaction. This highlights how subtle differences in system physics dictate the feasibility of quantum state preparation.
main_problem: The study analyzes the quantum control landscape for optimizing an observable by finding optimal external time-dependent controls $f(t)$ in specific four-level quantum systems.
main_result: The null control is proven to be a five-order trap, and the optimization efficiency shows a diverse behavior: sharp increases for V-V systems versus slower changes for chain interaction systems.
method: The work combines analytical proofs regarding the order of traps with numerical simulations using GRAPE (unconstrained) and GPM (constrained) algorithms.
model_or_system: The system involves four-level quantum dynamics governed by a Hamiltonian $H(t) = H_0 + f(t)V$. Specific models compared are a V-V type system and an anharmonic system with chain interaction.
key_observables: Optimization efficiency (fraction of successful runs), the objective functional $	ext{Tr}[U_f^T ho_0 U_f^\dagger T O]$, and the order of the control traps.
important_parameters: The initial control distance $l$ from the null control, and system-specific Hamiltonian parameters defining the V-V vs. chain interaction structure.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes controllability of the quantum system and relies on Taylor expansion methods to define trap orders.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate energy level structures for the two systems (V-V and chain), and show the fraction of failed runs versus initial control distance $l$ for both optimization methods.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the theoretical framework by proving the null control is a high-order trap. It then proceeds to numerical experiments comparing GRAPE and GPM performance on two distinct four-level models, highlighting quantitative differences in efficiency behavior.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the practical limitations of quantum control theory by quantifying how system structure dictates optimization success near degenerate or trapped points, which is crucial for designing robust quantum protocols.
